Elongated flying vehicle that accelerates by expelling high-speed exhaust and carries all of its own propellant.

A [[Rocket engine|rocket engine]] produces thrust by reaction to exhaust expelled at high speed. Unlike [[Jet engine|jet engines]], rockets need no oxygen from the air, so they can fly in the vacuum of space and operate more efficiently outside the atmosphere. Multistage rockets can reach [[Escape velocity|escape velocity]] from Earth. Chemical rockets, the most common high-power type, burn fuel with an oxidizer; the propellant may be a monopropellant, hypergolic liquids, kerosene (RP1) with liquid oxygen, a solid fuel, or a hybrid of solid fuel and liquid or gaseous oxidizer. The name comes from the Italian *rocchetta*, "bobbin" or "little spindle", after the shape.

Gunpowder rockets evolved in medieval China under the [[Song dynasty|Song dynasty]] by the 13th century, and the Mongols carried the technology to the Middle East and Europe in the mid-13th century. Rockets served as incendiary weapons in sieges. Hasan al-Rammah's book, written between 1270 and 1280, included 107 gunpowder recipes, 22 of them for rockets. The Mysorean rockets of the late 18th century, developed under [[Hyder Ali]], were the first successful iron-cased rockets. Sir William Congreve's British rocket of 1804, based directly on them, was fielded in the [[Napoleonic Wars|Napoleonic Wars]]; together the innovations raised effective range from 100 to 2,000 yards (91 to 1,829 m). William Leitch first proposed rockets for human spaceflight in 1861.

Modern rocketry rests on Konstantin Tsiolkovsky's 1903 theory of liquid-propellant rockets and Robert Goddard's 1926 launch of the first liquid-fueled rocket, which reached 12.5 m. The German V-2, developed by [[Wernher von Braun]], reached 80 km during World War II. Postwar rockets launched Sputnik 1 in 1957 and, in 1969, the [[Apollo 11]] mission to the Moon. Rockets are now used for fireworks, missiles, ejection seats, launch vehicles, human spaceflight, and space exploration.

Mountain range, western North America, the largest mountain system on the continent.

The Rockies stretch 3,000 mi (4,800 km) in a straight line from northern Western Canada to New Mexico in the southwestern United States, varying in width from 110 to 480 km (70 to 300 miles). They are the easternmost portion of the North American Cordillera and older than the Cascade Range and [[Sierra Nevada]], which lie farther west. Definitions of the northern end differ. Canadian geographers place it at the Liard River in northern [[British Columbia]], while the Geological Society of America definition also counts more northerly ranges as the "Arctic Rockies". The southern end lies near Albuquerque, close to the Rio Grande rift.

The system comprises dozens of subranges divided by high basins and wide tablelands. Most of the highest summits are in [[Colorado]]; Mount Elbert, at 4,401 m (14,440 ft), is the highest peak, and Mount Robson, at 3,954 m (12,972 ft), is highest in the Canadian Rockies. The Continental Divide of the Americas runs through the range, separating waters flowing to the Atlantic and Pacific. Triple Divide Peak (2,440 m) in Glacier National Park sends water to both oceans and to Hudson Bay. In Alberta, rivers feed the basin of the [[Mackenzie River]], which empties into the Beaufort Sea.

The Rockies formed 55 million to 80 million years ago during the Laramide orogeny, when plates began sliding at a shallow angle beneath the North American plate. Tectonic activity, erosion, and [[Glacier|glaciers]] have since sculpted the peaks and valleys. Humans began inhabiting the range at the end of the last ice age. The [[Lewis and Clark Expedition]] and Sir Alexander Mackenzie explored it, and minerals and the [[Fur trade|fur trade]] drove early economic exploitation, though the population has never been dense. The English name is a calque of the Plains Cree *asinîwaciy*. Public parks and forests protect much of the range, which draws visitors for hiking, mountaineering, skiing, and fishing.

Mammals of the order Rodentia, characterized by a single pair of continuously growing incisors in each jaw.

Rodents make up about 40% of all mammal species and are native to every major landmass except Antarctica. The name comes from Latin *rodens*, "gnawing". Most are small, with robust bodies, short limbs, and long tails, and most eat plant material. Enamel covers only the front of each incisor, so the softer dentine behind wears away faster and leaves a chisel-like edge; the animals must gnaw constantly to keep the teeth from growing so long that they pierce the skull. Rodents have no canines and a gap, the diastema, between incisors and cheek teeth, which lets them block out inedible material while gnawing. Species have 12–28 teeth in total.

Size ranges from most species weighing under 100 g (3.5 oz) to the [[Capybara|capybara]], the largest, at up to 66 kg (146 lb). Rodents live in nearly every terrestrial habitat and can be arboreal, burrowing, leaping, or semiaquatic; locomotion includes running, climbing, swimming, bipedal hopping, and gliding. They tend to be social, and mating systems range from monogamy to promiscuity. Many species bear underdeveloped young, while others bear relatively well-developed ones.

The fossil record begins in the Paleocene of Asia, and rodents diversified greatly in the [[Eocene]]. They reached South America and [[Madagascar]] from Africa and, until humans arrived, were the only terrestrial placental mammals to colonize Australia. Rodentia and [[Lagomorpha]] (rabbits, hares, and pikas) are sister groups forming the clade Glires; lagomorphs are distinguished by an extra pair of upper incisors.

Humans use rodents for food, clothing, pets, and laboratory research. The [[Brown rat]], the black rat, and the [[House mouse]] are serious pests that spoil stored food and spread disease, and introduced rodents are often invasive. Familiar rodents include mice, rats, squirrels, [[Beaver|beavers]], [[Guinea pig|guinea pigs]], and [[Hamster|hamsters]].

Artistic and intellectual movement originating in Europe toward the end of the 18th century.

Romanticism advocated subjectivity, imagination, and appreciation of nature in response to the [[Age of Enlightenment]] and the [[Industrial Revolution]]. Its adherents rejected social conventions in favor of individualism, argued that passion and intuition were crucial to understanding the world, and held that beauty evokes a strong emotional response rather than residing in form alone. Recurring themes included reverence for nature and the supernatural, idealization of the past, fascination with the exotic and mysterious, and celebration of the heroic and the sublime. Romantics were particularly fond of the [[Middle Ages]], which they saw as an era of chivalry and a more organic relationship between people and environment, in contrast to an industrial society they considered alienating. Critics have countered that such portrayals overlooked the downsides of medieval life.

The first Romantic ideas arose from the German Counter-Enlightenment movement *Sturm und Drang* ("Storm and Stress"), which questioned the claim that humans can fully comprehend the world through reason alone. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's *The Sorrows of Young Werther* (1774) helped shape the movement, and many early Romantics sympathized with the aims of the [[French Revolution]]. The movement is generally considered to have peaked from 1800 to 1850. In literature it is associated with William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge, whose *Lyrical Ballads* appeared in 1798; in painting with [[Caspar David Friedrich]] and J.M.W. Turner; and in music with [[Ludwig van Beethoven]] and [[Franz Schubert]].

Its decline in the mid-19th century followed the rise of Realism and Naturalism, Charles Darwin's *On the Origin of Species*, a more conservative political climate, and growing attention to the effects of technology and urbanization on the working class. By World War I it had dispersed into later movements, though Late Romantic and Neoromantic currents persisted. Romanticism influenced conservatism, liberalism, radicalism, nationalism, and modern conservation efforts.

City (pop. 2.7 million), capital of Italy and of the Lazio region.

Rome is a special municipality, Roma Capitale, covering 1,287.36 sq km. It is the third most populous city in the [[European Union]] within city limits, and its metropolitan city, with 4.2 million people, is the most populous in Italy. It lies in the central-western [[Italy|Italian]] peninsula along the Tiber Valley. Vatican City, the smallest country in the world and seat of the [[Catholic Church]] under the [[Holy See]], is an independent state within its boundaries. Rome is called the "City of Seven Hills", the "Eternal City" (Latin *Urbs Aeterna*), and *Caput Mundi* ("Capital of the World").

Roman mythology dates the founding of the city to around 753 BC, but archaeological evidence of human occupation goes back about 14,000 years. The early population mixed Latins, Etruscans, and Sabines. Rome became successively the capital of the Roman Kingdom, the Roman Republic, and the [[Roman Empire]]. In 192 the emperor [[Commodus]] renamed it Colonia Lucia Annia Commodiana, but the name reverted after his assassination that year. After the fall of the western Empire, Rome fell under the political control of the papacy and in the 8th century became capital of the [[Papal States]], which lasted until 1870. From the [[Renaissance]] onward, popes pursued an architectural and urban program over four hundred years, and Rome became a center of the Renaissance and the birthplace of the Baroque style and Neoclassicism. It became capital of the Kingdom of Italy in 1871 and of the Italian Republic in 1946. It hosted the Summer Olympics in 1960.

In 2019 Rome received 8.6 million tourists, ranking 14th among the world's most visited cities. Its historic center is a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site. The city hosts UN agencies, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme, as well as the headquarters of Italian companies such as Eni and Enel, and the Cinecittà film studios.

Persian-language Sufi mystic and poet, founder of the Mevlevi Order.

Jalāl al-Dīn Muḥammad Balkhī, known as Rumi, came from a family of Balkh and was born to Persian parents in Wakhsh, in present-day [[Tajikistan]]. His name means "from Rum", the Anatolian region once held by the [[Byzantine Empire]]; in Iran he is also called Mawlānā, "our master". His father, Bahā ud-Dīn Walad, was a preacher and jurist. Mongol advances forced the family west, and after stays in cities across Iran, [[Baghdad]], and Damascus, Rumi settled in Konya, in the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, at age 19. Besides his father, his most important influences were the Persian poets Attar and Sanai.

Rumi was expected to follow his father as an Islamic scholar, but the arrival in Konya of the wandering dervish Shams Tabrīzī changed his life. The two became deeply attached, and Rumi neglected his duties. When Shams disappeared, Rumi's intense grief found expression in the *Divan of Shams Tabrīzī*, which marked the beginning of his poetic output. The *Divan* is a collection of lyrical ghazals celebrating ecstatic love of the divine.

His six-volume *Masnavi*, of over 25,000 rhyming couplets, is often called a "Qur'an in Persian" and is considered one of the greatest poems of the [[Persian literature|Persian language]]. Many Muslims, particularly in the Turko-Persian cultural sphere, rank it among the most important works of Islamic literature, behind only the [[Quran]]. His prose discourses are collected in *Fihi ma Fihi*. His teachings present adversity, pain, and loss as paths to spiritual growth, and distinguish worldly love from true divine love.

Rumi died in Konya and was buried beside his father, and his shrine became a place of pilgrimage. After his death his followers and his son Sultan Walad founded the Mevlevi Order, known as the Whirling Dervishes for its *Sama* ceremony. His poems have been translated into many languages, and he has been described as the "world's most popular poet" and, in recent years, as the best-selling poet in the United States.

Country (pop. over 140 million) spanning Eastern Europe and North Asia, the largest in the world by area.

Russia, officially the Russian Federation, covers 17,098,242 sq km, spans eleven time zones, and shares land borders with fourteen countries. It is the most populous country in Europe and the ninth most populous in the world, with three-fourths of its people in urban areas. [[Moscow]] is the capital and largest city; [[Saint Petersburg]] is the second largest. Terrain ranges from tundra and taiga in the north to steppe and mountains in the south.

The East Slavs emerged as a prominent group between the 3rd and 8th centuries AD, leading to [[Kievan Rus']] in the 9th century, which adopted Orthodox Christianity from the Byzantine Empire in 988. After Kievan Rus' disintegrated in the 12th century, the Grand Principality of Moscow led the unification of Russian lands, culminating in the Tsardom of Russia in 1547. Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721. The Russian Revolution of 1917 abolished the monarchy, and after the Russian Civil War, Russia became the principal constituent of the [[Soviet Union]], founded in 1922. Millions died under [[Joseph Stalin]] during rapid industrialization in the 1930s. The Soviet Union played a decisive role for the Allies on the Eastern Front in World War II, competed with the United States as a superpower in the [[Cold War]], and launched the first artificial satellite and the first human expedition into outer space.

The Russian Federation emerged from the Soviet Union's dissolution in 1991. A constitution adopted after the 1993 crisis established a semi-presidential republic. Since the turn of the century the political system has been dominated by [[Vladimir Putin]], under whom Russia has experienced democratic backsliding and has come to be classified as authoritarian. Russia fought a war with Georgia in 2008 and has been at war with [[Ukraine]] since 2014, including the annexation of Crimea that year, which most UN member states do not recognize, and a full-scale invasion in 2022.

Russia holds the largest stockpile of nuclear weapons and a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Its economy relies on oil and natural gas. It has 32 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

East Slavic language of the Balto-Slavic branch of the Indo-European family.

Russian is the native language of the Russian people and one of four extant East Slavic languages, alongside Belarusian, Rusyn, and Ukrainian. It was the de facto official language of the Soviet Union and remains official in Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan. It has constitutional status as the language of inter-ethnic communication in Tajikistan and serves as a lingua franca in Ukraine, Moldova, the Caucasus, Central Asia, and, to a lesser extent, the Baltic states and Israel. It has over 210 million total speakers. It is the most spoken native language in Europe, the most spoken Slavic language, and the most geographically widespread language of Eurasia; it ranks seventh worldwide by native speakers and eleventh by total speakers. Russian is one of the six official languages of the UN and one of two on the International Space Station.

It is written in the Russian alphabet of the [[Cyrillic script]]. Most consonants have "hard" and "soft" counterparts, a distinction usually shown in writing by changing the following vowel. Unstressed vowels are reduced, and stress, often unpredictable, is not normally marked, though an optional acute accent can distinguish words such as *замо́к* (zamók, "lock") and *за́мок* (zámok, "castle"). Russian is a fusional language, in which one inflectional ending marks several grammatical features, and it uses prefixes and suffixes for word formation more than most Slavic languages.

The word *russky* derives from the ethnonym and toponym *Rus*. Church Slavonic, used as a literary language in the medieval period, gave Russian many borrowings and calques ultimately from Greek. The Old Novgorod dialect is sometimes thought to have contributed to its formation. Over centuries, vocabulary was also influenced by Polish, Dutch, German, French, Italian, and English, and to a lesser extent by Turkic, Persian, [[Arabic]], and Hebrew. It became a standardized literary medium in the 18th century through reforms by figures such as [[Mikhail Lomonosov]].

City (pop., 2025: 11.9 million), capital of São Paulo state and the largest city in Brazil.

São Paulo, Portuguese for "Saint Paul", is the most populous city in the Americas and the most populous Portuguese-speaking city in the world. Its residents are called *paulistanos*. Greater São Paulo has more than 20 million inhabitants, and the surrounding Macrometropolis, the first megalopolis in the Southern Hemisphere, has more than 30 million. The city lies on a highland plateau about 800 m above sea level, roughly 70 km inland from the port of Santos, and covers about 1,521 sq km.

Jesuit priests founded the city in 1554, making it one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on the American continents. Before the Europeans arrived, the Piratininga plains were inhabited by Tupi peoples. During the colonial period it was the starting point for expeditions of the Paulista *bandeirantes*, who expanded the country's territory and economy. Its wealth was consolidated during the Brazilian coffee cycle of the mid-19th century, and industrialization in the 20th century made it the main national economic hub. Waves of immigration produced a cosmopolitan population that includes the largest Arab, Italian, and Japanese diasporas in the world. Landmark events in Brazilian history staged there include the Cry of Ipiranga, the Modern Art Week, the 1932 Revolution, and the *Diretas Já* movement.

São Paulo is the largest urban economy in Latin America, accounts for around 10% of Brazilian GDP, and is the headquarters of B3, the largest stock exchange in Latin America by market capitalization. The University of São Paulo is often considered the best in Brazil and Latin America. The city's growth has also brought income disparities, informal settlements, chronic traffic, and pollution.

Cultural institutions include Ibirapuera Park, the São Paulo Museum of Art, and the Pinacoteca. Events include the São Paulo Art Biennial and São Paulo Fashion Week. The city hosted the 1950 and 2014 FIFA World Cups and hosts the annual Brazilian Grand Prix of [[Formula One]].

Emotional pain associated with feelings of loss, despair, grief, helplessness, disappointment, and sorrow.

A person experiencing sadness may become quiet or lethargic and withdraw from others; crying can be an indication. Severe sadness is exemplified by depression, a mood that can result from major depressive disorder or persistent depressive disorder, though normal sadness is temporary and differs from clinical depression. Sadness is one of the six basic emotions described by Paul Ekman, along with happiness, anger, surprise, fear, and disgust. Typical triggers are perceived loss, such as a death or separation, and failure to achieve personal goals.

Functional theories hold that sadness serves two primary purposes in coping with loss. One is to promote cognitive changes that restructure beliefs and goals; sad people tend to be less affected by general schemas, including political ones. The other is to signal a need for assistance and elicit support from others, and shared sadness may increase relationship building. Brain studies associate sadness with activity in the temporal cortex, lateral cerebellum, midbrain, putamen, and caudate, and, in studies using film clips, with increases in the prefrontal cortex and thalamus.

In childhood, sadness is a common experience and part of separating from the mother and becoming independent. Robin Skynner argued that treating sadness as "not allowed" can leave people shallow and manic, and T. Berry Brazelton argued that too much cheering up devalues the emotion. Margaret Mahler saw the capacity to feel sadness as an emotional achievement.

Coping methods include seeking social support, spending time with a pet, and creating a list. Strategies such as ruminating or permanent isolation can prolong sadness. Cognitive behavioral therapy suggests challenging negative thoughts or scheduling positive events. Pupil size is also an indicator: sad faces with small pupils are judged more intensely sad, and viewers' own pupils shrink in response, a mirroring that predicts higher empathy scores.
